report:
## Conclusion: the claim is supported, not false

The best direct evidence is the ACTIVE trial: a large randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of daily 80-µg abaloparatide in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. Over 18 months, it found fewer *new morphometric vertebral fractures* with abaloparatide than placebo, and the authors concluded that abaloparatide reduced new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures. This is strong evidence for the stated claim.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2544640

The U.S. prescribing information likewise states that, in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, abaloparatide reduces vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk—an indication based principally on the pivotal clinical-trial evidence.  
https://www.tymloshcp.com/tymlos-prescribing-information.pdf

A 2024 systematic review also concluded that abaloparatide has a protective effect in postmenopausal osteoporosis and can reduce vertebral-fracture risk. This is supportive, though the underlying pivotal trial remains the most informative evidence.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307725/

**Important qualifications:** the evidence concerns women with established osteoporosis who were at elevated fracture risk, treatment for 18 months, and radiographically detected (“morphometric”) new vertebral fractures. It does not mean every postmenopausal woman benefits equally, or that treatment is risk-free; prescribing decisions must weigh adverse effects, contraindications, cost, and alternative therapies.
